title: Lost in Delegation: Studying the Effectiveness of Task Orchestration in Generative Search
trick: Split a multi-fact web-search question into per-fact subagent calls with the same model and it answers no better, and worse on post-cutoff facts, because the brief adds wrong guesses and the return hides failures.
framing_stripped: Called 'studying the effectiveness of task orchestration in generative search' with 'purpose-built datasets with pre- and post-cutoff splits' and a 'delegation boundary'; it is a 4 x 4 x 4 x 2 grid (configurations: no tool / single agent / forced delegation / optional delegation; models: Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking; datasets: Books, Nobel, GDP, Products; facts before or after every model's cutoff) scored by item-level accuracy, where orchestrator and executor are the same model and the orchestrator sees only the executor's final answer; the headline is that delegation is worse than direct tool use in 21-22 of 32 cells and loses about 10 points post-cutoff while the single agent loses 2 (Tables 1-2), followed by four LLM-judged failure rates (added-and-wrong attributes in the brief, redundant searches, lower accuracy after a 403 the orchestrator never sees, re-delegation of correct answers) and two prompt fixes that do not close the gap (sec. 6).
method_equations: Configurations (sec. 3; Table 8; App. A): (1) no tool, a single model answers closed-book; (2) single agent, the same model with web_search (SerpAPI Google results: titles, URLs, snippets) and open_url (truncated Markdown of a page); (3) forced delegation, an orchestrator with no search tool 'break[s] the problem down into atomic subproblems' and must call call_subagent for each; the executor is the same model in a fresh context with web_search and open_url and returns only its final answer, 'The orchestrator receives neither the executor's intermediate trajectory nor the contents returned by its web tools' (App. A); (4) optional delegation, the orchestrator may instead answer a subtask from memory. Datasets (sec. 3; Table 6): each prompt asks for several independently verifiable time-stamped facts; the splitting variable is a year. Books (Goodreads Top 100; pre-cutoff 2014-2019, $N = 120$ prompts, $n = 585$ items after 15 titles with mismatched years were removed; post-cutoff 2026, $N = 20$, $n = 100$; 5 items per prompt). Nobel (Nobel Prize API; pre 2014-2019, $N = 34$, $n = 72$; post 2025-2026, $N = 12$, $n = 24$; 1-3 laureates). GDP (World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, growth to one decimal; 2019 vs 2025; $N = 30$, $n = 120$ each; the same 30 four-country sets, 'prompts differ only in the year'). Products (iF Design Award; launched 2021 vs 2026; $N = 30$, $n = 120$ each; 4 items). Pre-cutoff years precede every reported cutoff (Jun 2024 to Jul 2025, Table 5). Metric (sec. 3): $$\mathrm{Acc} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{M_i} \sum_{j=1}^{M_i} \mathbf{1}_{ij},$$ where $N$ is the number of prompts, $M_i$ the number of items in prompt $i$ and $\mathbf{1}_{ij} = 1$ when item $j$ of prompt $i$ is correct (GDP: within 0.1 percentage points of ground truth); 95% percentile bootstrap intervals over prompts with $B = 1000$ resamples. Budgets (sec. 3; Table 7): with $n$ items per prompt the single agent gets $2n$ web_search and $3n$ open_url calls; the orchestrator gets $2n$ call_subagent calls and every executor a fresh 2 web_search + 3 open_url, so the delegated arm may issue up to $4n$ searches and $6n$ page opens against the single agent's $2n$ and $3n$ (Books: 10/15 vs 10 calls x 2/3); failed calls outside the model's control do not count; tokens are neither budgeted nor reported. Headline (Table 1, mean over four models and four datasets, pre $\to$ post): no tools $0.53 \to 0.01$; single agent $0.77 \to 0.75$; optional delegation $0.74 \to 0.64$; forced delegation $0.77 \to 0.66$; 'the gap to direct tool use increases from 1 to 9 pp for forced delegation and from 3 to 11 pp for optional delegation' (sec. 4). Per cell (Table 2, 32 model x dataset x cutoff cells): optional delegation below the single agent in 22 (above in 7, tied 3), forced below in 21 (above 10, tied 1). Largest losses, GPT-5 post-cutoff GDP $0.89 \to 0.43$ (optional) and $0.35$ (forced), GPT-5 post-cutoff Books $0.91 \to 0.52 / 0.60$; GPT-OSS pre-cutoff GDP $0.92 \to 0.65 / 0.73$. Gains: Qwen under forced delegation in 6 of 8 conditions (post-cutoff Products $0.33 \to 0.58$, pre-cutoff Nobel $0.82 \to 1.00$), Claude pre-cutoff Products $0.73 \to 0.89$. Under optional delegation the orchestrator answered 21% of items from memory (sec. 4). Failure modes. (a) Brief distortion (sec. 5.1, Books only, judge gpt-5.6-luna with the prompt in App. B): share of first briefs (single agent: first search query) that add an attribute absent from the user prompt, Figure 2; GPT-5 adds a medium to up to 98% of pre-cutoff forced briefs; correctness of what was added, Table 3 (% correct, pre $\to$ post): GPT-5 medium $93 \to 6$ (forced), $76 \to 4$ (optional), author $95 \to 0$ and $84 \to 0$; GPT-OSS medium $58 \to 21$ (forced), author $72 \to 0$; Claude medium $64 \to 0$ (forced), $70 \to 0$ (optional); Qwen medium $69 \to 22$ (forced); 'delegation adds only incorrect author information on the post-cutoff split'. (b) Redundant search (sec. 5.2): 40% of item-level trajectories contain more than one search; of 5,577 consecutive query pairs 9% are judged 'the same search'; 7% under direct tool use vs 11% under delegation, driven by GPT-5 ($8\% \to 19\%$); Qwen 19% on Products and 31% on Nobel; multi-item briefs (Table 4, % of executor requests): GPT-OSS 4.5 (optional) / 2.7 (forced), GPT-5 3.2 / 0.9, Qwen 0.0, Claude 0.4 / 0.6. (c) Failure recovery (sec. 5.3): open_url returns 403 on 13% of single-agent calls vs 20% (optional) and 17% (forced), empty content 3% vs 5% / 5%; accuracy on items hit by a 403: 73% single vs 54% forced vs 52% optional; after empty content 60% vs 50% vs 45%. (d) Return handling (sec. 5.4; Figure 4; judge labels accepted / questioned / questioned-then-used / rejected / no reaction, App. B): challenging rises $2.6\% \to 3.2\%$ pre $\to$ post, immediate re-delegation $6.6\% \to 8.6\%$; challenging a correct executor answer 0.3% / 0.2%; re-delegating a correct answer $6.4\% \to 8.8\%$; GPT-5 re-delegates up to 54% of tasks on pre-cutoff GDP. Mitigations (sec. 6; App. C): a no-repeat instruction leaves the same-search share at $19.4\% \to 17.7\%$ (Qwen) and $4.4\% \to 6.6\%$ (GPT-5) on Books; an instruction to report inaccessible URLs moves GDP accuracy for GPT-5 from $0.43 \to 0.51$ (optional) and $0.35 \to 0.44$ (forced) against a single-agent 0.89, and for GPT-OSS from $0.70 \to 0.62$ and $0.73 \to 0.64$. Judge validation (App. C.1): 104 Books query pairs, three authors, Fleiss $\kappa = 0.78$; the judge matches the majority on 97% of 102 pairs, $\kappa = 0.65$; only the same-search judge is validated.
load_bearing_assumption: That single agent vs forced delegation isolates the delegation boundary: 'Complementing these studies, we isolate the effect of delegating tool access on performance' (sec. 2); 'delegation frequently reduces accuracy despite providing access to the same external tools' (sec. 4). The two arms are not otherwise equal. (i) Budget: the single agent has $2n$ searches and $3n$ opens for the whole prompt; the delegated system has $2n$ executors each with 2 searches and 3 opens, up to twice the retrieval (Table 7), and tokens and model calls are uncounted. (ii) Instruction: the single agent is told 'If you do not know the answer to a question, use the web_search tool', the executor 'Use them judiciously and only call a tool if you are not sure of the answer. If you know the answer and think the tool will not provide any additional information, do not use it' (Table 8), a stronger push toward answering from memory, in a study whose post-cutoff condition is designed so memory is wrong. (iii) The per-fact rewriting step exists only in the delegated arms; the paper's own account of the headline ('Query rewriting can alter the task itself', sec. 5.1) is a property of asking a model to restate a fact request, which a single agent that writes a search query also does (Figure 2 shows single agents add attributes too, less often). If the ~10-point post-cutoff loss is produced by (i)-(iii) rather than by the separation of contexts, then 'the delegation boundary ... hinder[s] recovery' (sec. 7) is not what was measured. Second, that post-cutoff items are unknown to the models: supported by closed-book accuracy of 0-6% post-cutoff (Table 2), with Qwen's cutoff reported as a release date (Table 5), 'The actual knowledge cutoff may therefore be earlier' (App. A).
weakest_component: The attribution from failure rates to the accuracy gap. Sections 5.1-5.4 report four rates (added-and-wrong attributes, same-search pairs, 403s and conditional accuracy, challenge and re-delegation) and the conclusion says these 'may contribute to the observed lower accuracy' (sec. 5.3); no decomposition states how many of the lost items had a distorted brief, a hidden failure or a discarded correct return, and the brief-distortion measurement exists for Books only. Next: (1) the mean in Table 1 averages models with opposite signs, GPT-5 loses up to 54 pp while Qwen gains in 6 of 8 forced conditions (sec. 4), so 'delegation often reduces accuracy' is mostly a GPT-5 and GPT-OSS result; (2) the 22-of-32 and 21-of-32 counts include cells whose 95% intervals overlap (Claude Books pre 0.85 [0.80, 0.89] vs 0.83 [0.79, 0.87]); the post-cutoff Books and Nobel sets are 20 and 12 prompts (Qwen Nobel post 0.28 [0.03, 0.53]); (3) every behavioural number is an LLM judge (gpt-5.6-luna, same family as two of the four studied models) and only the same-search judge was checked against humans (App. C.1); the attribute-addition and challenge judges are unvalidated; (4) sampling at temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0 with reasoning effort medium (App. A), number of runs per cell unknown (not in text), so intervals cover prompt resampling and not run-to-run variance; (5) tool-call counts are shown only as figures (Figures 7-8) and tokens never, so the compute of each arm is unknown; (6) the executor budget (2 searches, 3 opens) is tighter per fact than the single agent's pooled budget, while the system total is looser, so budget cuts both ways and neither direction is controlled.
regime: Models: claude-sonnet-4-5 (cutoff Jan 2025), gpt-5 (Sep 30, 2024), openai/gpt-oss-120b (Jun 1, 2024), Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (release Jul 31, 2025); orchestrator and executors always the same model (Table 5; App. A). Sampling: temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0, reasoning effort medium for closed models; open models on vLLM on H200 GPUs (App. A). Tool: one web interface, SerpAPI Google search plus open_url (truncated Markdown). Configurations: 4 (no tool, single agent, forced delegation, optional delegation); the orchestrator has no search tool and receives final answers only. Datasets: 4, all time-stamped facts, 214 pre-cutoff and 92 post-cutoff prompts in total (Books 120/20, Nobel 34/12, GDP 30/30, Products 30/30), 897 pre-cutoff and 364 post-cutoff scored items, 1-5 items per prompt (Table 6). Horizon: at most $2n$ searches and $3n$ opens per prompt ($n = 3$-$5$), 2 searches and 3 opens per executor (Table 7). Accuracy bands (Table 2): single agent 0.30-1.00 pre, 0.28-1.00 post; closed-book 0.18-0.93 pre, 0.00-0.06 post. Judge: gpt-5.6-luna, 2,000 output tokens, 5,577 consecutive query pairs judged; 104 pairs human-annotated (App. B, C.1). Repeats per cell, token counts, API cost: unknown (not in text). Code and data release: unknown (not in text). arXiv v1, 12 Nov 2026; venue not stated.
information_asymmetry: The asymmetry runs both ways across the boundary. Downward: the orchestrator holds the user's wording, the sibling items and its parametric beliefs; the executor receives only the rewritten brief, so a folded-in belief ('the song "The Night We Met" by Lord Huron' for a 2026 novel, sec. 5.1) becomes the executor's task, and it cannot tell a guess from a given. Upward: the executor sees the search results, the opened pages, the 403s and contradicting evidence ('encountered evidence for the correct 2026 book three times', sec. 5.1); the orchestrator receives 'neither the executor's intermediate trajectory nor the contents returned by its web tools' (App. A), so a failure, a source or the executor's uncertainty reaches it only if the executor writes it, and the orchestrator weighs a bare answer against its own belief ('Subagent is wrong', sec. 5.4). Measured directly: downward distortion, as the share of first briefs adding medium or author and the correctness of each addition (Figure 2, Table 3), Books only, by LLM judge. Measured only by proxy: the upward loss. Failure visibility is read from accuracy conditional on a 403 (73% vs 54% / 52%, sec. 5.3), never from the return message (did it name the failed URL, cite a source, state confidence); re-delegation and challenge rates (sec. 5.4) are reactions to the return, not measurements of it. Nothing is counted in tokens: context saved, tokens per arm, brief and return lengths are absent although context cost is the stated motivation (sec. 1). The missing ruler is per-return: which of source, failure and confidence from the trace survived into the reply, and whether the orchestrator's answer changes when those fields are injected or stripped, swept between 'final answer only' and 'complete executor traces' (sec. 7) at matched tool and token budgets, with the unmatched budgets (Table 7) and executor prompt (Table 8) removed first.
occupies: Published: that with orchestrator and executor the same model (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking), per-fact delegation of web lookups beats direct tool use in only 7-10 of 32 model x dataset x cutoff cells and loses about 10 points of accuracy from pre- to post-cutoff facts while the single agent loses 2 (Tables 1-2); the pre/post-cutoff paired-dataset design for delegation (Books, Nobel, GDP, Products); four LLM-judged failure rates (post-cutoff briefs add wrong authors and media, 9% same-search pairs, lower accuracy after a 403 the orchestrator cannot see, re-delegation of 6-9% of correct returns); and the negative result that a no-repeat instruction and a report-failures instruction do not close the gap. Not claimed and left open: matched tool-call or token budgets between arms; any measurement of the return message's content (source, failure, confidence) or of tokens saved; attribution of lost items to the four modes; heterogeneous orchestrator-executor pairs; interdependent subtasks; more than one run per cell.

neighbors.title: Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
neighbors.trick: Hold reasoning tokens equal and a single agent matches or beats multi-agent systems on multi-hop reasoning, argued from the data-processing inequality (a message between agents can only lose information) and tested on Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Gemini 2.5; cited here as 'multi-agent setups often fail to outperform single-agent baselines' (sec. 2), and this paper moves the question to tool-mediated retrieval of post-cutoff facts without matching budgets.

neighbors.title: Can Small Agents Collaborate to Beat a Single Large Language Model?
neighbors.trick: One orchestrator over small specialised subagents with restricted communication beats a much larger single model with tools on tool-heavy QA, with orchestrator capacity driving the gain and subagent reasoning adding little or less; this paper's same-model orchestrator-executor pairs are the control that removes the size difference and finds no gain.

neighbors.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
neighbors.trick: Annotate 1,600+ traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks into a 14-mode failure taxonomy (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification) with an LLM judge checked against humans; this paper measures four of these shapes as rates on controlled per-fact search tasks instead of annotating existing frameworks.

neighbors.title: LiveBrowseComp: Are Search Agents Searching, or Just Verifying What They Already Know?
neighbors.trick: Show search agents answer up to 44.5% of BrowseComp closed-book and write most queries from internal hypotheses, then build a 90-day-recent benchmark where closed-book accuracy falls under 2% and rankings change; this paper borrows the recency split and shows the same knowledge dependence moving into the orchestrator's briefs under delegation.

neighbors.title: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate -- We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
neighbors.trick: Evaluate 5 multi-agent debate methods on 9 benchmarks with 4 models and find debate rarely beats chain-of-thought or self-consistency while spending more compute, with model heterogeneity the one reliable fix; this paper is the same null result for tool delegation and leaves heterogeneous pairings to future work (sec. 7).

theme_fit.why: the orchestrator brief and the executor return are the lane's object, costed here in accuracy (about 10 points post-cutoff) with the downward loss measured as a quantity (added attributes and their correctness, Table 3) and the upward loss only inferred (accuracy after a 403, re-delegation of correct returns); the measurement the lane wants, what the return carries vs what the trace held at matched budgets, is the gap the paper leaves

an attribution-of-outcome question (orchestrator vs executor vs tool) with an unmatched comparison: delegation has up to twice the search budget and a different tool-use instruction (Tables 7-8), tokens are uncounted, one run per cell at temperature 1.0, and the behavioural rates come from an LLM judge of which only one is human-validated
context growth and KV-cache cost are the stated motivation for delegation (sec. 1) but no token, cache or latency number is measured; the cost side of the trade-off is asserted, not shown

limitations_as_complaints: My delegation study only ever asks for facts that do not depend on each other, so I cannot say what the boundary costs when one subagent's answer is the next subagent's input: 'we focus on small datasets of independent factual questions. Real-world tasks may consist of interdependent information needs. We deliberately study this simpler setting to test delegation without the additional challenges of task interdependence. Failures in these simpler settings raise concerns about generalizability to more complex settings' (sec. 7, Limitations).

My orchestrator and my executor are always the same model, so a cheap executor under a strong orchestrator, the configuration people actually deploy, is unmeasured: 'we study configurations in which orchestrators and executors belong to the same model family. We do so to avoid a combinatorial explosion of heterogeneous setups. Studying the interplay between different model families is an interesting avenue for future work' (sec. 7, Limitations).

I know the return message loses the failures and the sources, but I never measured what it should carry or what that costs in tokens; I only tried one prompt and the full-trace extreme is ruled out by assumption: 'Instructing executors to report failures yields only limited improvements. Passing complete executor traces to the orchestrator could mitigate the loss of information, but would undermine the context-saving benefits of delegation' (sec. 7); 'Addressing this challenge may require targeted mechanisms for communicating evidence and resolving conflicts rather than simple prompt interventions' (sec. 6) [paraphrase: no token count, brief or return length, or intermediate disclosure level appears in the text].
